subject: Medieval History
sub_topic: Iqta system — comparison across Sultanate rulers

concepts.name: Origin and Pre-Sultanate Antecedents of the Iqta System
key_dimensions: Abbasid Caliphate roots and its transfer to the Indian subcontinent via the Ghaznavids and Ghurids
Distinction between the Central Asian iqta and the Indian adaptation — structural and functional divergence
Whether Qutb-ud-din Aibak or Iltutmish should be credited with formalizing the system in India
Comparison with pre-existing Indian land assignment systems (e.g., vishti, bhoga) to identify what was truly new

concepts.name: Structural Definition of Iqta: Land Assignment vs. Revenue Assignment
key_dimensions: Iqta as a revenue-yielding assignment (not ownership) — the critical legal distinction UPSC exploits
Difference between iqta, jagir, and watan — overlapping terms and their dynasty-specific usage
Non-hereditary nature of early iqta vs. gradual hereditary tendencies — a key evolutionary trap
Relationship between iqta and military obligation (fief-like but not feudal in the European sense)

concepts.name: Iltutmish and the Systematization of the Iqta System
key_dimensions: Iltutmish's role in transforming ad hoc assignments into a regularized administrative-military instrument
Creation of the Turkan-i-Chahalgani (Forty) and their connection to iqta grants as a power consolidation tool
Central supervision mechanisms introduced by Iltutmish — the role of the central diwan
How Iltutmish used iqta to integrate the Turkish nobility and suppress rival power centers

concepts.name: The Muqti/Wali: Role, Powers, and Accountability of the Iqta Holder
key_dimensions: Dual function of the muqti — revenue collection AND military recruitment/maintenance
Obligation to maintain a fixed quota of cavalry (hasham) from iqta revenues
Accountability mechanisms: the concept of 'fawazil' (surplus after expenses) to be remitted to the sultan
Distinction between muqti, amil, and khut/muqaddam — UPSC frequently conflates these roles

concepts.name: Balban's Reforms of the Iqta System: Centralization and Military Discipline
key_dimensions: Balban's policy of resuming iqtas from Turkish nobles who had become autonomous — deliberate recentralization
Introduction of rigorous 'chehra' (branding of horses) and 'dagh' (muster rolls) to audit military strength funded by iqtas
Balban's use of spies (barid) to monitor muqtis — the surveillance dimension of iqta control
Tension between Balban's centralization and the Turkish nobility's expectation of hereditary iqtas

concepts.name: Alauddin Khalji's Radical Overhaul of the Iqta System
key_dimensions: Alauddin's market reforms (price control) and their direct link to reducing the cash value of iqtas — the salary-in-kind paradox
Shift toward cash salaries (naqd) vs. iqta assignments — Alauddin's partial move to a salaried army and its limits
Resumption of iqtas granted to religious classes (waqf, milk) — conflict with ulema
Impact of Alauddin's revenue reforms (direct state collection) on the functional scope of the muqti

concepts.name: Muhammad bin Tughluq and the Iqta System: Experimentation and Instability
key_dimensions: Expansion of the empire and the challenge of assigning iqtas in distant Deccan territories
Muhammad bin Tughluq's token currency experiment and its catastrophic effect on iqta revenue valuation
Introduction of new categories of assignees and the resulting administrative confusion
How the Doab taxation policy intersected with and undermined the iqta framework in core territories

concepts.name: Firuz Shah Tughluq and the Hereditary Iqta: Feudalization Debate
key_dimensions: Firuz Shah's formal recognition of hereditary succession of iqtas — the single most important departure from the original system
Allowing sons/slaves to substitute for aging iqta holders — practical military implications
Whether this represents 'feudalization' — historiographical debate (Irfan Habib vs. others)
Long-term consequence: weakening of central authority and the road to the Sultanate's decline

concepts.name: Iqta System under the Early Khiljis (Jalal-ud-din Khalji): Transition Period
key_dimensions: Jalal-ud-din's conciliatory approach — restoration of some iqtas to displaced Turkish nobles
The tension between continuity (Slave dynasty iqta norms) and the Khalji revolution in governance
How the Khalji transition affected the composition of iqta holders (shift from Turkish exclusivity)
Jalal-ud-din as a bridge figure — often overlooked in UPSC answers but critical for periodization

concepts.name: The 'Fawazil' Mechanism: Surplus Revenue and Central Control
key_dimensions: Definition: the surplus remaining after a muqti meets military obligations from iqta revenue
Central state's claim on fawazil — the theoretical check on muqti autonomy
Practical failure of fawazil collection as the Sultanate weakened — a symptom of declining central authority
Comparison: how different sultans enforced or ignored fawazil remittance (Iltutmish strict; Firuz Shah lax)

concepts.name: Iqta vs. Jagir vs. Waqf: Distinguishing Land Assignment Categories
key_dimensions: Iqta (military-administrative assignment), jagir (later Mughal term, often conflated), and inam/milk (religious/personal grants) — definitional precision
Waqf as a religious endowment vs. iqta as a state instrument — key difference in revocability
UPSC trap: anachronistic use of 'jagir' for the Sultanate period — when does the term legitimately apply
Overlap between iqta and the concept of 'khalisa' (crown land) — what was NOT given as iqta

concepts.name: Military Dimension of the Iqta: Cavalry Quotas and the Conditional Nature of the Grant
key_dimensions: The contractual logic: iqta granted in exchange for maintaining a specified number of armed horsemen
How sultans verified compliance — muster reviews, dagh system under Balban and Alauddin
Consequence of non-compliance — threat of resumption (though rarely fully enforced)
Comparison with European feudal military obligation — similarities and critical differences (no liege loyalty chain)

concepts.name: Administrative Role of the Muqti Beyond Revenue: Justice, Law and Order, and Local Governance
key_dimensions: Muqti as the de facto governor of the iqta territory — civil and military functions combined
Limits on judicial authority — serious cases referred to the sultan's court (qazi network)
Tension between muqti's local power and the central state's claim to sovereignty (kharaj collection oversight)
How the muqti system created proto-provincial administration — a precursor to the Mughal subah system

concepts.name: Geographic Variation in Iqta Administration: Core vs. Peripheral Territories
key_dimensions: Difference in iqta functioning between the Gangetic heartland (tightly controlled) and frontier regions (semi-autonomous)
Bengal and distant provinces — iqta holders as virtually independent rulers during weak sultans
The Deccan expansion under Alauddin and the challenge of assigning viable iqtas in newly conquered zones
How geographic distance inherently undermined the fawazil and accountability mechanisms

concepts.name: Historiographical Debate: Was the Iqta System 'Feudal'?
key_dimensions: Irfan Habib's thesis: Indian feudalism with iqta as evidence — key arguments and their basis
Counter-arguments: Mohammad Habib, A.L. Srivastava — iqta as a non-feudal, centralized instrument
The Burton Stein 'segmentary state' model and why it does NOT apply to the Sultanate's iqta system
UPSC angle: questions framing iqta as 'feudal' — how to nuance the answer with historiographical awareness

concepts.name: Iqta and the Peasantry: Extraction Mechanisms and Agrarian Impact
key_dimensions: The muqti's relationship with local intermediaries (khuts, muqaddams, chaudharis) — who actually extracted revenue
Alauddin's attempt to eliminate the khut-muqaddam layer and collect directly — revolutionary but short-lived
Impact of iqta transfers (frequent reassignment) on agrarian investment and stability
Distinction between kharaj (land tax) rates in iqta vs. khalisa lands — was there a differential burden on peasants?

concepts.name: Decline of the Iqta System and Its Legacy in the Lodi Sultanate
key_dimensions: Lodi period: iqta system largely replaced by Afghan tribal chieftaincy arrangements — 'afghan polity' model
How Firuz Shah's hereditary grants set the structural conditions for Sayyid and Lodi period fragmentation
Whether the Mughal mansabdari system was a reformation or rejection of the iqta model
Legacy question: elements of iqta that survived in Mughal jagir — continuity vs. rupture in land assignment history

concepts.name: Iqta System and the Role of the Central Diwan (Finance Department)
key_dimensions: The Diwan-i-wizarat's role in assigning, reassigning, and auditing iqtas — the bureaucratic backbone
Wazir's power to recommend iqta grants vs. sultan's ultimate authority — checks and overlaps
How a strong wazir (e.g., under Iltutmish) enhanced central control over iqtas; how a weak one enabled muqti autonomy
The diwan-i-arz (military department) vs. diwan-i-wizarat in iqta oversight — jurisdictional division

concepts.name: Women and Succession in the Iqta System: The Raziyya Period and Gender Dimensions
key_dimensions: Whether female sultans (Raziyya) could grant and revoke iqtas with full legitimacy — a legitimacy-authority nexus question
Turkish nobles using control of iqtas as leverage against Raziyya's reign — iqta as political weapon
Succession disputes and iqta redistribution as a mechanism of political realignment after a sultan's death
UPSC angle: questions on Raziyya often ignore the iqta-political economy connection — a high-yield integration point
